title: Baba Deep Singh the scholar
hookLine: before his last ride, tradition says he spent years copying the Granth at Damdama

lines: A LAMP, A REED PEN, A PAGE.
cards: A lamp, a low desk, a sheet of paper, a pot of ink, a reed pen. An old man bends over the page and forms one Gurmukhi letter, then the next. Outside, Punjab is full of horsemen and burning villages.

In here it's quiet, except for the scratch of the pen. Sikhs know how Baba Deep Singh's story ends: the old warrior on his last ride to Amritsar. This lesson stays with the years before it, at the desk.

teach.b: The place was Damdama Sahib, at Talwandi Sabo, in the dry south of Punjab.
Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh stayed there after years of war, and that the Granth was written out there in its full form, with Bhai Mani Singh as scribe and Baba Deep Singh beside him.
Tradition says Baba Deep Singh stayed on after the Guru left, teaching, and copying the Granth by hand so more sangats could have it. There's no printing press.

teach.h: EVERY COPY MADE LETTER BY LETTER.
teach.b: Every copy of the Guru's word is made one letter at a time, and a slip of attention puts a word wrong. So the copyist has to be slow, steady and humble before the text, for years.
Guru Nanak has a line about writing that fits this desk exactly.

teach.h: LOVE THE PEN, THE MIND THE WRITER.
teach.b: In paraphrase, from the Granth: burn away worldly attachment and grind it into ink; make your understanding the paper; make love the pen and the mind the writer; then ask the Guru, and write the Name.
For Guru Nanak that's a picture of the inner life. At Damdama it was also an actual workday. Then look at his hands.

teach.h: THE PEN, AND LATER THE SWORD.
teach.b: The same hands that held the pen would later hold a sword. Sikhs call people like him scholar-warriors, and they don't treat the two halves as a contradiction.
The Khalsa's ideal, in a phrase Sikhs use, is sant-sipahi, saint-soldier. Baba Deep Singh's last ride makes sense because of the desk.
He knew exactly what the Harmandir and the Guru's word meant, letter by letter, because he had copied it.

how: Sikhs honor Damdama Sahib at Talwandi Sabo as a seat of Sikh learning, and remember Baba Deep Singh both as a copyist of the Guru Granth Sahib and as a martyr.

o: a soldier who gives up prayer to take up the sword
saint-soldier, the Khalsa's ideal of scholar and fighter
a holy man who refuses ever to carry a weapon

games.q: the scholar at the desk — tap the pairs.
p: the pen, in Guru Nanak's line

s: Baba Deep Singh was only a warrior
tradition says he spent years at Damdama Sahib copying the Granth by hand before his last ride.
in Guru Nanak's line, love is the pen and the mind is the writer
and worldly attachment is burned and ground into ink.
Sikhs see the scholar and the warrior in him as a contradiction
Sikhs speak of the sant-sipahi, saint-soldier, as one ideal.

games.q: you're Baba Deep Singh. the Guru has left Damdama, and the land outside is full of danger. what do you do with your days?
o: ride out at once to fight.
stay, teach, and copy the Granth so more sangats can have it.
go home and keep out of it.
games.why: tradition says he stayed at Damdama, teaching and copying the Granth by hand, before his last ride years later.

practice: With a pen and any scrap of paper, write out one line from your own tradition's scripture, or, if you don't have one, the opening words of the Granth: Ik Oankar, one God.
Write it slower than feels natural, each letter a whole breath, and notice your attention when your hand has to be careful. If you pray, say Waheguru as you set the pen down.

wordCard.voice: Sant-sipahi, saint-soldier, the Khalsa's ideal that Baba Deep Singh lived at Damdama Sahib, the same hands that held the pen later holding the sword.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Baba Deep Singh; Baba, elder, is a title of love and respect.

carryVoice: Your line: the scholar-warrior. Slow, careful work can be the ground courage stands on. Day eight hundred sixty-two.

sources.ref: Baba Deep Singh at Damdama Sahib, Sikh tradition
